title: Always there
hook: women's stories were often unrecorded, but they were always there

segments.voice: Yesterday was antisemitism today, and the line was hate returns, courage too. Did you check on someone, or did someone check on you? Today a new stretch of the story begins, with the people the record kept leaving out. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

Open the book of Exodus to its first chapter. A king of Egypt orders that every Hebrew baby boy be killed at birth. The text never tells us that king's name. He is just Pharaoh. But two women stand between his order and the babies, and the text names them both: Shiphrah and Puah, the midwives. The man with the throne goes unnamed, and two women who deliver babies get their names written down. Hold that picture, because for long stretches of the history we've been walking through, it ran the other way. Today's title is about the women who were there the whole time: always there.
screen: `A KING WITH NO NAME.` → `TWO MIDWIVES, NAMED.` → `THE RECORD OFTEN RAN THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Here is what the midwives did. "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive." A quiet refusal, inside a birthing room, by women who had no army. The Torah remembers it. Later books remember more women by name: Miriam with her timbrel at the sea, Deborah judging Israel under a palm tree, Ruth on the road, Esther in the palace. Now step out of the Bible and into the long centuries after it. Much of what was written down in those centuries was written by men, about the things men argued over in the study house and the court. A great deal of women's lives went unrecorded. Who lit the candles each Friday in a cold room. Who ran the shop while her husband studied. Who kept the family's recipes, songs and accounts, and taught a child the first blessing. Those lives were rarely signed. But the record leaves traces. In the margins of old books, in letters, in the memoir a merchant woman named Glikl wrote in Yiddish for her children. In prayers in Yiddish, written for women to say over the candles and the dough. Historians have spent a long time gathering those traces. So the line for today isn't a complaint and it isn't a slogan. It's a correction to how we read. When a page of history seems to be all men, it often means the women were in the next room, keeping the whole thing alive, and nobody was taking notes. Over the next days you'll meet some of them by name: a seamstress who started a school, a rabbi, a girl at a lectern, a writer, a teacher. They didn't appear from nowhere. They were always there.
screen: `THE MIDWIVES SAID NO.` · `NAMED IN THE BIBLE.` · `UNRECORDED FOR CENTURIES.` · `TRACES IN LETTERS AND PRAYERS.` · then, large: `ALWAYS THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one woman's story, starting with one you already half know. Sit comfortably, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a woman from your own family line, or someone else's: a grandmother, a great-aunt, a neighbor who raised half the street. What do you actually know about her? Her name. Where she lived. One thing she made, or said, or kept. Notice where your knowledge stops. That edge is where her story went unrecorded. Rest with her for a while, just as she was. Later today, if you can, ask someone one question about her. The bell holds the time.
Always there. The women of Jewish history, from the midwives of Exodus to the grandmothers no one wrote about, present the whole time, even where the record left them out. Today's word.
Your line: nobody was taking notes. Today, when you read or hear a story with only men in it, ask once where the women were. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish communities and schools increasingly teach women's history alongside the familiar story, reading the women of the Bible closely and gathering the letters, memoirs and Yiddish prayers that women left behind.

fork.setup: you're a Hebrew midwife in Egypt. the king has ordered you to kill every baby boy you deliver. what do you do?
options: obey, because he is the king.
quietly refuse, and let the babies live.
run away and leave the women alone.
fork.reveal: they refused: "the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive." and the text writes down their names.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jewish history is mostly a story about men.
what it means: women were there all along, often unrecorded, lighting the candles, running the shop, teaching the first blessing.
what a scholar hears: the traces in the margins, the letters, Glikl's memoir, the Yiddish prayers for women, and a Bible that names two midwives and not the king.
